newsitem.title: FRANCE: LVMH raises Grand Met stake over 10 pct.
newsitem.headline: LVMH raises Grand Met stake over 10 pct.

text.p: France's LVMH raised its stake in Grand Metropolitan to more than 10 percent on Tuesday, turning up the pressure on GrandMet and its merger partner Guinness to agree to LVMH's plan for a three-way drinks combination, market sources and analysts said.
LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton declined to disclose its holding in GrandMet but confirmed that it bought GrandMet shares and sold some of its 14.2 percent Guinness stake.
Share analysts said LVMH's move suggested it had reached an impasse with the heads of the British companies and was threatening to take its alternative plan to the shareholders.
"It looks like the British managers are holding out," said one Paris-based analyst.

With a 10 percent holding in GrandMet, LVMH may call an extraordinary general meeting of GrandMet shareholders. If it lines up enough allies in the group to form a 25 percent block, it could stop the 24 billion pound merger announced in May.

The Guinness and GrandMet chairmen, who have met twice recently with LVMH chairman Bernard Arnault, were expected to reply to his proposal to set up a listed company blending their respective drinks activities as early as Wednesday after a Guinness board meeting.
Arnault quit the Guinness board to show his discontent with the management's lack of support for his plan.

LVMH declined to comment on reports that Arnault was travelling to Britain this week to try to convince holders of Guinness's and GrandMet's dispersed capital that his plan would generate more value than the creation of a sprawling drinks, beer, canned goods and fast foods conglomerate.

Arnault's plan would establish a drinks group with more than 60 billion francs ($9.9 billion) in sales and a portfolio ranging from Hennessy cognacs and Moet Chandon champagnes to GrandMet's Smirnoff, Gilbey's, J&B and Bailey's brands and Guinness's Johnnie Walker, Dewar's, Gordon and Tanqueray drinks.

He proposes to put LVMH's 66 percent stake in Moet Hennessy, its 14.2 percent stake in Guinness and newly acquired 6.4 percent holding in GrandMet into the new drinks company whose market capitalisation is estimated at roughly 70 billion francs.
Arnault signalled this week that he was flexible on one of the potential sticking points -- his stake in the new drinks company.
LVMH initially floated the prospect of a 35 percent stake but now says that, depending on the valuations, it may take less.
"LVMH said it would have 35 percent of the new drinks company, Guinness said LVMH's holdings would give it only 25 percent, and it will end up being around 30 percent," said a Paris-based analyst.
"I think he'll further refine his offer. He might reduce it to 30 percent. My feeling is that we'll see a spirits company floated. I believe that will happen," said an analyst in London.

"I think he has leverage with shareholders in both companies. There are two things he has to do -- show that there are tangible synergies, which there are, and come up with a reasonable price for Moet Hennessy which he is in the process of doing. If the price is reasonable, shareholders will line up with Arnault," the analyst said.
Arnault opposes the GrandMet-Guinness merger which risked marginalising LVMH's drinks business and locking up part of its capital in an unlisted subsidiary of the new GMG Brands.
Last month LVMH spent more than eight billion francs to buy 6.4 percent of Grand Met, becoming its largest shareholder as well as the leading shareholder in Guinness.

The French company previously launched legal action against Guinness to claim the right to buy it out of the valuable distribution ventures they share if it merged with GrandMet. Those ventures hold the rights for 10 years to market Guinness brands in France, the United States and much of the Far East.
Guinness shares fell 11 pence to 598, and Grand Met stock rose 15-1/2 pence to 630 on Tuesday.
LVMH's stock fell 0.32 percent to 1,559 francs in a market that rose 1.64 percent.
